authors: Shunyu Yao, Jeffrey Zhao, Dian Yu, Nan Du, Izhak Shafran, Karthik Narasimhan, Yuan Cao
title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
shows: Interleaves reasoning traces with actions that query external sources, and reports gains over reasoning-only and acting-only baselines on HotpotQA, FEVER, ALFWorld and WebShop. It is the template for the observe-think-act loop that most tool-using agents implement.

authors: Timo Schick, Jane Dwivedi-Yu, Roberto Dessì, Roberta Raileanu, Maria Lomeli, Luke Zettlemoyer, Nicola Cancedda, Thomas Scialom
title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
shows: Trains a language model to decide when and how to call external APIs using self-generated training data. It frames tool use as a learned capability and motivates the function-calling interfaces used today.

authors: Theodore R. Sumers, Shunyu Yao, Karthik Narasimhan, Thomas L. Griffiths
title: Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents
shows: Proposes the CoALA framework, organizing language agents by memory modules, action space and decision procedure, and links them to classic cognitive architectures. It gives a vocabulary for describing and comparing the design of a personal agent.

authors: Noah Shinn, Federico Cassano, Edward Berman, Ashwin Gopinath, Karthik Narasimhan, Shunyu Yao
title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
shows: Agents store verbal self-critiques of failed attempts in an episodic memory buffer and use them on later trials, improving task success without weight updates. It is the standard reference for reflection-based learning from feedback.

authors: Charles Packer, Sarah Wooders, Kevin Lin, Vivian Fang, Shishir G. Patil, Ion Stoica, Joseph E. Gonzalez
title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
shows: Manages a hierarchy of memory tiers by letting the model move information between in-context and external storage through function calls. It is a concrete design for long-term memory in assistants that run over long periods.

authors: Joon Sung Park, Joseph C. O'Brien, Carrie J. Cai, Meredith Ringel Morris, Percy Liang, Michael S. Bernstein
title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
shows: Describes an architecture with a memory stream, retrieval scored by recency, importance and relevance, reflection, and planning, evaluated in a simulated town. Its retrieval-and-reflection design is widely reused for agent memory.

authors: Patrick Lewis, Ethan Perez, Aleksandra Piktus, Fabio Petroni, Vladimir Karpukhin, Naman Goyal, Heinrich Küttler, Mike Lewis, Wen-tau Yih, Tim Rocktäschel, Sebastian Riedel, Douwe Kiela
title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
shows: Introduces retrieval-augmented generation, combining a parametric generator with a non-parametric retrieved document index. It underlies approaches to grounding an agent in a user's mail, files and notes.

authors: Yunfan Gao, Yun Xiong, Xinyu Gao, Kangxiang Jia, Jinliu Pan, Yuxi Bi, Yi Dai, Jiawei Sun, Meng Wang, Haofen Wang
title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
shows: Surveys naive, advanced and modular RAG pipelines, covering retrieval, generation and augmentation techniques and evaluation. Useful as a map of design choices for a personal-data retrieval layer.

authors: Akari Asai, Zeqiu Wu, Yizhong Wang, Avirup Sil, Hannaneh Hajishirzi
title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
shows: Trains a model to decide when to retrieve and to critique its own retrieved passages and outputs using reflection tokens. It shows adaptive retrieval as an alternative to always retrieving a fixed number of passages.

authors: Jason Wei, Xuezhi Wang, Dale Schuurmans, Maarten Bosma, Brian Ichter, Fei Xia, Ed Chi, Quoc Le, Denny Zhou
title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
shows: Shows that giving worked intermediate reasoning steps in the prompt improves performance on arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic tasks in large models. It is the basis for the reasoning component of later agent loops.

authors: Shunyu Yao, Dian Yu, Jeffrey Zhao, Izhak Shafran, Thomas L. Griffiths, Yuan Cao, Karthik Narasimhan
title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
shows: Generalizes chain-of-thought to a search over branching reasoning steps with self-evaluation and backtracking. It illustrates deliberate planning with lookahead as opposed to a single left-to-right pass.

authors: Guanzhi Wang, Yuqi Xie, Yunfan Jiang, Ajay Mandlekar, Chaowei Xiao, Yuke Zhu, Linxi Fan, Anima Anandkumar
title: Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
shows: An agent in Minecraft that accumulates a library of executable skills it writes and reuses, with iterative prompting from execution feedback. It is an example of procedural memory stored as code.

authors: Nelson F. Liu, Kevin Lin, John Hewitt, Ashwin Paranjape, Michele Bevilacqua, Fabio Petroni, Percy Liang
title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics (arXiv:2307.03172)
shows: Finds that model accuracy on retrieval-style tasks depends on where relevant information sits in a long context, and is often lower for information in the middle. It is evidence for ordering and trimming what an agent places in context.

authors: Prithvi Rajasekaran, Ethan Dixon, Carly Ryan, Jeremy Hadfield, et al. (Anthropic Applied AI team)
title: Effective context engineering for AI agents
shows: Practitioner account of managing what goes into the context window across long-running agent tasks, including just-in-time retrieval, compaction and sub-agents. Assigned as a current statement of context management practice from a model maker.

authors: Anthropic
title: Introducing Contextual Retrieval
shows: Describes a retrieval preprocessing method that prepends chunk-specific context before embedding and indexing. Relevant to indexing personal documents where isolated chunks lose meaning.

authors: Erik S., Barry Zhang (Anthropic)
title: Building effective agents
shows: Distinguishes fixed workflows from agents and describes patterns such as prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers and evaluator-optimizer. It recommends using the simplest structure that works and is the baseline practitioner reference for the course.

authors: Jeremy Hadfield, Barry Zhang, Kenneth Lien, Florian Scholz, Jeremy Fox, Daniel Ford
title: How we built our multi-agent research system
shows: Engineering account of an orchestrator with parallel sub-agents for research tasks, including prompting, evaluation and reliability lessons. It gives concrete evidence on when sub-agent designs help and what they cost.

authors: Walden Yan (Cognition)
title: Don't Build Multi-Agents
shows: Argues from the practitioner side that sub-agents can act on inconsistent context, and discusses sharing full traces. Assigned as a counterpoint to multi-agent designs.

authors: Ken Aizawa et al. (Anthropic)
title: Writing effective tools for agents — with agents
shows: Guidance on designing, describing and evaluating tools so that agents use them correctly, including how tool outputs consume context. Directly applicable to designing mail, calendar and CRM tools.

authors: Bin Wu et al. (Anthropic)
title: Introducing advanced tool use on the Claude Developer Platform
shows: Describes a tool search tool that discovers tools on demand instead of loading all definitions, plus programmatic tool calling and tool-use examples. It addresses context cost when an agent has many tools.

authors: Model Context Protocol project
title: Model Context Protocol Specification (version 2025-06-18)
shows: The protocol specification for connecting LLM applications to tools, resources and prompts over JSON-RPC, with client features such as sampling and elicitation and stated consent and security principles. It is the primary source on the tool-interface standard.

authors: Model Context Protocol project
title: Model Context Protocol Specification: Tools (2025-06-18)
shows: Specifies tool listing, calling, input and output schemas, annotations, error handling and the human-in-the-loop and security requirements. Read alongside tool-design guidance when defining agent tools.

authors: OpenAI
title: Function calling (also known as tool calling)
shows: Documents the tool-calling flow: send tool definitions, receive a tool call, run it in application code, return the output and receive a final answer or further calls. A vendor reference for the loop in practice.

authors: OpenAI
title: A Practical Guide to Building AI Agents
shows: Covers when to build an agent, design of models, tools and instructions, orchestration from single-agent loops to multi-agent setups, and layered guardrails including human intervention for high-risk actions. Page opened is the web version, dated January 15, 2026 on the page; the original PDF appeared in April 2025 per a secondary source.

authors: Shishir G. Patil, Tianjun Zhang, Xin Wang, Joseph E. Gonzalez
title: Gorilla: Large Language Model Connected with Massive APIs
shows: Fine-tunes a model to write API calls from a large set of documented APIs using retrieval over documentation. Relevant to selecting among many tools and avoiding invalid calls.

authors: Yujia Qin, Shihao Liang, Yining Ye, Kunlun Zhu, Lan Yan, Yaxi Lu, Yankai Lin, Xin Cong, et al.
title: ToolLLM: Facilitating Large Language Models to Master 16000+ Real-world APIs
shows: Builds a dataset and evaluation over more than 16,000 real REST APIs, with an API retriever to choose tools for an instruction. It is early work on tool retrieval from large tool sets.

authors: Shunyu Yao, Noah Shinn, Pedram Razavi, Karthik Narasimhan
title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
shows: Benchmarks agents that converse with a simulated user while calling domain tools under policy rules, and measures consistency over repeated trials. It tests the setting closest to an assistant acting for a person.

authors: Grégoire Mialon, Roberto Dessì, Maria Lomeli, Christoforos Nalmpantis, Ram Pasunuru, Roberta Raileanu, et al.
title: Augmented Language Models: a Survey
shows: Surveys language models augmented with reasoning skills and the ability to use tools. A broad entry point to the literature before ReAct-style agents.

authors: Lei Wang, Chen Ma, Xueyang Feng, Zeyu Zhang, Hao Yang, Jingsen Zhang, et al.
title: A Survey on Large Language Model based Autonomous Agents
shows: Surveys LLM agents by profile, memory, planning and action modules, plus applications and evaluation. Gives a structured overview of the field.

authors: Lilian Weng
title: LLM Powered Autonomous Agents
shows: An overview essay by a practitioner covering planning, memory and tool use components of LLM agents with references to the primary papers. Useful as an orientation reading.

authors: Prateek Chhikara, Dev Khant, Saket Aryan, Taranjeet Singh, Deshraj Yadav
title: Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory
shows: Presents a memory layer that extracts, consolidates and retrieves facts from conversations, with evaluation on a long-conversation benchmark. The authors are the system's developers, so results should be read as vendor-reported.

authors: Richard C. Atkinson, Richard M. Shiffrin
title: Human Memory: A Proposed System and Its Control Processes
venue: In K. W. Spence and J. T. Spence (eds.), The Psychology of Learning and Motivation, vol. 2, Academic Press, pp. 89-195 (confirmed via the 2016 Cambridge University Press reprint listing)
shows: The multi-store model of sensory registers, short-term store and long-term store with control processes. It is the source of the working-memory versus long-term-memory split that agent memory designs borrow.

authors: Eric Horvitz
title: Principles of Mixed-Initiative User Interfaces
shows: Sets out principles for combining automated services with direct user control, using the Lookout meeting-scheduling system as an example, including reasoning about the costs and benefits of acting. It is the foundational reference for proactive assistants that decide when to act or ask.

authors: Qingyun Wu, Gagan Bansal, Jieyu Zhang, Yiran Wu, Beibin Li, Erkang Zhu, Li Jiang, et al.
title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
shows: A framework in which multiple conversable agents, tools and humans exchange messages to complete tasks. Representative of conversation-based multi-agent orchestration.

authors: Sirui Hong, Mingchen Zhuge, Jiaqi Chen, Xiawu Zheng, Yuheng Cheng, Ceyao Zhang, et al.
title: MetaGPT: Meta Programming for A Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework
shows: Assigns role-specific agents standardized operating procedures and structured intermediate outputs for software tasks. Illustrates role-based decomposition in multi-agent systems.

authors: Shuyan Zhou, Frank F. Xu, Hao Zhu, Xuhui Zhou, Robert Lo, Abishek Sridhar, Xianyi Cheng, Tianyue Ou, Yonatan Bisk, Daniel Fried, Uri Alon, Graham Neubig
title: WebArena: A Realistic Web Environment for Building Autonomous Agents
shows: A self-hostable environment of functional websites and long-horizon web tasks judged on outcome. It showed a large gap between agents and humans and remains the standard benchmark for browser agents.

authors: Xiang Deng, Yu Gu, Boyuan Zheng, Shijie Chen, Samuel Stevens, Boshi Wang, Huan Sun, Yu Su
title: Mind2Web: Towards a Generalist Agent for the Web
shows: A dataset of tasks over many real websites with recorded action sequences, used to study generalization to unseen sites and domains. It frames how HTML is pruned and ranked for an LLM.

authors: Boyuan Zheng, Boyu Gou, Jihyung Kil, Huan Sun, Yu Su
title: GPT-4V(ision) is a Generalist Web Agent, if Grounded
shows: Evaluates a multimodal model as a web agent and finds that converting its planned action to a concrete page element (grounding) is the main bottleneck. It motivates attention to grounding strategy in screen-driven agents.

authors: Tianbao Xie, Danyang Zhang, Jixuan Chen, Xiaochuan Li, Siheng Zhao, Ruisheng Cao, et al.
title: OSWorld: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Open-Ended Tasks in Real Computer Environments
shows: A benchmark of open-ended tasks executed in real operating systems and applications with execution-based scoring. It measures how far screenshot-based agents are from human performance on desktop work.

authors: Jianwei Yang, Hao Zhang, Feng Li, Xueyan Zou, Chunyuan Li, Jianfeng Gao
title: Set-of-Mark Prompting Unleashes Extraordinary Visual Grounding in GPT-4V
shows: Overlays numbered marks on image regions so a multimodal model can refer to them, improving visual grounding. The technique is used to let screenshot agents name which element to click.

authors: Yujia Qin, Yining Ye, Junjie Fang, Haoming Wang, Shihao Liang, Shizuo Tian, et al.
title: UI-TARS: Pioneering Automated GUI Interaction with Native Agents
shows: Presents a model trained end-to-end to perceive screenshots and act on GUIs, as opposed to an agent assembled from prompted general models. Representative of the native GUI-agent approach.

authors: Anthropic
title: Introducing computer use, a new Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Claude 3.5 Haiku
shows: Announces a public-beta API in which a model views screenshots and issues cursor and keyboard actions, with an OSWorld result and a statement that the capability is error-prone. A primary source for the vendor computer-use interface.

authors: Anthropic
title: Computer use tool (Claude API documentation)
venue: Anthropic platform documentation (page as fetched in November 2026)
shows: Documents the screenshot-mouse-keyboard agent loop, batching, screenshot scaling, and security guidance such as using a sandboxed VM, allowlisting domains, human confirmation of consequential actions, and prompt-injection risk from web content. Documentation changes over time; cite the access date.

authors: Grégoire Mialon, Clémentine Fourrier, Craig Swift, Thomas Wolf, Yann LeCun, Thomas Scialom
title: GAIA: a benchmark for General AI Assistants
shows: A set of real-world questions that need tool use, browsing and multimodal reasoning, easy for humans but hard for tool-augmented models. A reference for evaluating general assistants.

authors: John Yang, Carlos E. Jimenez, Alexander Wettig, Kilian Lieret, Shunyu Yao, Karthik Narasimhan, Ofir Press
title: SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
shows: Shows that the design of the interface between model and computer (commands, feedback format, guardrails) changes agent performance on software tasks. It is the main evidence for treating tool-interface design as a first-class problem.

authors: Geewook Kim, Teakgyu Hong, Moonbin Yim, Jeongyeon Nam, Jinyoung Park, Jinyeong Yim, et al.
title: OCR-free Document Understanding Transformer
shows: An end-to-end model that reads document images and outputs structured text without a separate OCR stage. It frames the OCR-pipeline versus vision-language-model choice for invoices, receipts and attachments.

authors: Yupan Huang, Tengchao Lv, Lei Cui, Yutong Lu, Furu Wei
title: LayoutLMv3: Pre-training for Document AI with Unified Text and Image Masking
shows: Pre-trains a model jointly on text, layout and image patches for document tasks, using OCR-derived words as input. Representative of the OCR-plus-layout approach that contrasts with OCR-free models.

authors: Lukas Blecher, Guillem Cucurull, Thomas Scialom, Robert Stojnic
title: Nougat: Neural Optical Understanding for Academic Documents
shows: A visual transformer that converts page images of documents, including math and tables, to markup text. An example of model-based PDF-to-text conversion in place of classical OCR.

authors: Manuel Faysse, Hugues Sibille, Tony Wu, Bilel Omrani, Gautier Viaud, Céline Hudelot, Pierre Colombo
title: ColPali: Efficient Document Retrieval with Vision Language Models
shows: Retrieves documents by embedding page images with a vision-language model instead of extracting text first, and introduces a benchmark for visually rich document retrieval. Relevant to indexing scanned and layout-heavy personal files.

authors: Alec Radford, Jong Wook Kim, Tao Xu, Greg Brockman, Christine McLeavey, Ilya Sutskever
title: Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision
shows: Trains a speech recognition model on 680,000 hours of weakly supervised multilingual audio and reports robust zero-shot transcription across datasets. It is the reference for voice input to personal assistants.

authors: OpenAI
title: Introducing Whisper
shows: Announcement of the open-source Whisper speech recognition system with its training data scale and supported tasks. The page itself notes it is an older post and points to current OpenAI audio models.

authors: Jerome H. Saltzer, Michael D. Schroeder
title: The Protection of Information in Computer Systems
shows: Sets out the design principles for protection mechanisms, including least privilege, complete mediation, fail-safe defaults, separation of privilege and psychological acceptability. A personal-agent permission gate is a direct application of these principles.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Norm Hardy
title: The Confused Deputy (or why capabilities might have been invented)
shows: Describes a privileged program that is tricked into misusing its own authority on behalf of a caller, and argues that authority should travel with the request as a capability. An LLM agent holding the user's mail and file credentials is a confused deputy by construction.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Jack B. Dennis, Earl C. Van Horn
title: Programming Semantics for Multiprogrammed Computations
shows: Introduces capability-style protection: unforgeable references that name an object and carry the right to use it. It is the origin of the capability model that later agent-security designs revive.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Butler W. Lampson
title: Protection
venue: 5th Princeton Conf. on Information Sciences and Systems (1971); reprinted ACM Operating Systems Review 8(1), 1974
shows: Formalises protection as an access matrix of subjects, objects and rights, from which access-control lists and capability lists are derived as column and row views. Gives students the vocabulary for stating what an agent may do to which resource.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Butler W. Lampson
title: A Note on the Confinement Problem
shows: States the problem of keeping a program from leaking information to anyone but its caller and shows leakage through covert and side channels. It frames why an untrusted model reading private data cannot simply be told not to leak it.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: James P. Anderson
title: Computer Security Technology Planning Study (ESD-TR-73-51)
venue: USAF Electronic Systems Division technical report
shows: The Anderson report, which introduced the reference monitor concept: a small, always-invoked, tamper-proof, verifiable mediator of every access. It is the classical statement of what a code-level permission gate between model and tools should be.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Dorothy E. Denning
title: A Lattice Model of Secure Information Flow
shows: Models information-flow policy as a lattice of security classes and derives rules for certifying that a program obeys it. It is the basis for label-based flow control such as that used in recent agent defences.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: D. Elliott Bell, Leonard J. LaPadula
title: Secure Computer Systems: Mathematical Foundations (MITRE MTR-2547, Vol. I)
shows: Gives the Bell-LaPadula confidentiality model (no read up, no write down). It explains why tainting an agent's context with private data should restrict where that context may later be written or sent.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Kenneth J. Biba
title: Integrity Considerations for Secure Computer Systems (MTR-3153)
shows: Defines integrity policies in which low-integrity data must not influence high-integrity objects, the dual of Bell-LaPadula. Prompt injection is an integrity-flow problem: untrusted text steering privileged actions.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Joseph A. Goguen, Jose Meseguer
title: Security Policies and Security Models
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
shows: Introduces noninterference: one group's actions must have no effect on what another group can observe. It is the formal property that dual-LLM and information-flow-control agent designs try to approximate.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Andrew C. Myers, Barbara Liskov
title: Protecting Privacy Using the Decentralized Label Model
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology 9(4)
shows: Presents labels that record data owners and permitted readers, with controlled declassification and static checking (Jif). It is a worked model for per-item provenance and reader labels on mail, calendar and CRM data.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Andrei Sabelfeld, Andrew C. Myers
title: Language-Based Information-Flow Security
venue: IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications 21(1)
shows: Surveys three decades of work on enforcing noninterference with type systems and program analysis, including implicit flows and covert channels. It is the standard entry point to the information-flow literature that agent-security work builds on.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: William Enck, Peter Gilbert, Byung-Gon Chun, Landon P. Cox, Jaeyeon Jung, Patrick McDaniel, Anmol N. Sheth
title: TaintDroid: An Information-Flow Tracking System for Realtime Privacy Monitoring on Smartphones
shows: Shows dynamic taint tracking of sensitive data through third-party apps at the sink where data leaves the device, with modest overhead and a documented weakness to implicit flows. It is a practical precedent for tracking taint from private sources to outbound agent tools.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Jerome H. Saltzer, David P. Reed, David D. Clark
title: End-to-End Arguments in System Design
shows: Argues that a function can be correctly provided only with knowledge at the endpoints, so lower layers supply it only as an optimisation. For agents it supports enforcing policy at the tool boundary rather than trusting the model to police itself.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Mark S. Miller, Ka-Ping Yee, Jonathan Shapiro
title: Capability Myths Demolished
venue: Johns Hopkins Systems Research Laboratory report SRL-2003-02
shows: Rebuts claims that capabilities are equivalent to ACLs, cannot enforce confinement, or cannot be revoked. It supports the capability-style, per-task authority designs used for delegating to agents.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Fabio Perez, Ian Ribeiro
title: Ignore Previous Prompt: Attack Techniques For Language Models
shows: An early systematic study of goal hijacking and prompt leaking against a deployed language model. It records the first public framing of the problem.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Kai Greshake, Sahar Abdelnabi, Shailesh Mishra, Christoph Endres, Thorsten Holz, Mario Fritz
title: Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
shows: Introduces indirect prompt injection, where instructions arrive in retrieved or tool-returned data rather than from the user, and shows it against real LLM-integrated applications. It defines the threat that mail- and file-reading agents face.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Yupei Liu, Yuqi Jia, Runpeng Geng, Jinyuan Jia, Neil Zhenqiang Gong
title: Formalizing and Benchmarking Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses
shows: Gives a formal framework for prompt injection and benchmarks several attacks and defences across models and tasks. It is a reference for how results are measured.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Edoardo Debenedetti, Jie Zhang, Mislav Balunovic, Luca Beurer-Kellner, Marc Fischer, Florian Tramer
title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
shows: A dynamic benchmark of agent tasks over mail, banking, travel and workspace tools with injection attacks and defences. Its task suites resemble personal-agent workloads and are the common yardstick for system-level defences.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Qiusi Zhan, Zhixiang Liang, Zifan Ying, Daniel Kang
title: InjecAgent: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool-Integrated Large Language Model Agents
shows: A benchmark of indirect injections in tool-integrated agents, separating attacks that harm the user directly from those that exfiltrate data. It shows base-rate vulnerability of tool-using models.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Hanrong Zhang, Jingyuan Huang, Kai Mei, Yifei Yao, Zhenting Wang, Chenlu Zhan, Hongwei Wang, Yongfeng Zhang
title: Agent Security Bench (ASB): Formalizing and Benchmarking Attacks and Defenses in LLM-based Agents
shows: A benchmark covering several attack types, including prompt injection, memory poisoning and tool attacks, across agent scenarios. It extends evaluation beyond injection into persistence attacks.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Eric Wallace, Kai Xiao, Reimar Leike, Lilian Weng, Johannes Heidecke, Alex Beutel
title: The Instruction Hierarchy: Training LLMs to Prioritize Privileged Instructions
shows: Trains models to rank system, user and tool-output instructions by privilege. A representative model-level defence, useful as a contrast with enforcement outside the model.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Keegan Hines, Gary Lopez, Matthew Hall, Federico Zarfati, Yonatan Zunger, Emre Kiciman
title: Defending Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks With Spotlighting
shows: Marks untrusted input with delimiters, datamarking or encoding so the model can tell it from instructions. A representative prompt-level mitigation that reduces but does not eliminate attack success.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Milad Nasr, Nicholas Carlini, Chawin Sitawarin, Sander V. Schulhoff, Jamie Hayes, Michael Ilie, Juliette Pluto, Shuang Song, Harsh Chaudhari, Ilia Shumailov, Abhradeep Thakurta, Kai Yuanqing Xiao, Andreas Terzis, Florian Tramer
title: The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections
shows: Applies adaptive optimisation and human red-teaming to twelve published defences and bypasses most with success rates above 90 percent, although they reported near-zero attack success in their own evaluations. It is the main evidence for not relying on model-level defences as the only control.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Narek Maloyan, Dmitry Namiot
title: Prompt Injection Attacks on Agentic Coding Assistants: A Systematic Analysis of Vulnerabilities in Skills, Tools, and Protocol Ecosystems
shows: A systematisation of injection attacks on agentic assistants organised by delivery vector, modality and propagation. Useful as a recent taxonomy of attack surfaces for tool-using agents.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Peiran Wang, Xinfeng Li, Chong Xiang, Jinghuai Zhang, Ying Li, Lixia Zhang, Xiaofeng Wang, Yuan Tian
title: The Landscape of Prompt Injection Threats in LLM Agents: From Taxonomy to Analysis
shows: A survey and taxonomy of prompt-injection threats in the agent execution loop with open problems. A reading-list entry for the state of the field.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Simon Willison
title: The Dual LLM pattern for building AI assistants that can resist prompt injection
shows: Proposes a privileged model with tools that never sees untrusted text and a quarantined model that reads untrusted text with no tools, joined by ordinary code. It is the origin of the pattern CaMeL later formalised.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Edoardo Debenedetti, Ilia Shumailov, Tianqi Fan, Jamie Hayes, Nicholas Carlini, Daniel Fabian, Christoph Kern, Chongyang Shi, Andreas Terzis, Florian Tramer
title: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design
shows: CaMeL extracts control and data flow from the trusted user request and enforces capability-style policies over values in a custom interpreter. It completes 77 percent of AgentDojo tasks with provable security, against 84 percent undefended, which makes it the central design reference for a permission gate.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Luca Beurer-Kellner, Beat Buesser, Ana-Maria Cretu, Edoardo Debenedetti, Daniel Dobos, Daniel Fabian, Marc Fischer, David Froelicher, Kathrin Grosse, Daniel Naeff, Ezinwanne Ozoani, Andrew Paverd, Florian Tramer, Vaclav Volhejn
title: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections
shows: Proposes principled design patterns for agents with provable resistance to prompt injection and analyses their utility and security trade-offs through case studies. A practical menu for structuring a personal agent.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Manuel Costa, Boris Kopf, Aashish Kolluri, Andrew Paverd, Mark Russinovich, Ahmed Salem, Shruti Tople, Lukas Wutschitz, Santiago Zanella-Beguelin
title: Securing AI Agents with Information-Flow Control
shows: Presents Fides, a planner that attaches confidentiality and integrity labels to data and deterministically enforces policy, evaluated on AgentDojo. It connects classical information-flow control to LLM agents.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Yuhao Wu, Franziska Roesner, Tadayoshi Kohno, Ning Zhang, Umar Iqbal
title: IsolateGPT: An Execution Isolation Architecture for LLM-Based Agentic Systems
shows: Applies OS-style execution isolation to separate apps in an LLM-based agent system, with mediated cross-app communication. A model for isolating third-party tools from each other.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Simon Willison
title: The lethal trifecta for AI agents: private data, untrusted content, and external communication
shows: Observes that an agent with private data, exposure to untrusted content and an outbound channel can be steered into leaking that data. It gives a compact test for whether a personal-agent configuration is exploitable.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Meta AI
title: Agents Rule of Two: A Practical Approach to AI Agent Security
shows: States that until injection can be reliably detected, an agent session should combine no more than two of: untrusted input, sensitive data or systems, and state change or external communication. It turns the trifecta into a design rule, with human approval as the usual way to drop a property.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Lisanne Bainbridge
title: Ironies of Automation
shows: Argues that automating most of a task leaves the human the hard residue while removing the practice needed to handle it, and that monitoring is a task people do poorly. It predicts why a human approving agent actions degrades over time.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Raja Parasuraman, Victor Riley
title: Humans and Automation: Use, Misuse, Disuse, Abuse
shows: Defines misuse (overreliance), disuse (neglect, often from false alarms) and abuse of automation. It is the standard reference for the two failure modes of agent approval prompts.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Raja Parasuraman, Dietrich H. Manzey
title: Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation: An Attentional Integration
shows: Reviews evidence that complacency and automation bias occur in experts and novices and are not removed by practice or simple instruction. It supports designing approvals that do not depend on sustained vigilance.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Joshua Sunshine, Serge Egelman, Hazim Almuhimedi, Neha Atri, Lorrie Faith Cranor
title: Crying Wolf: An Empirical Study of SSL Warning Effectiveness
shows: A survey and lab study finding that many users ignore or misunderstand SSL warnings and that redesigned warnings only partly help. It is evidence that frequent, generic confirmation dialogs are routinely clicked through.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Devdatta Akhawe, Adrienne Porter Felt
title: Alice in Warningland: A Large-Scale Field Study of Browser Security Warning Effectiveness
shows: Uses telemetry on over 25 million warning impressions to show click-through rates vary strongly with warning design, from about a tenth to over two thirds. It shows that approval prompt design, not only presence, determines whether humans act as a control.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Dick Hardt (ed.)
title: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework (RFC 6749)
shows: Specifies the authorization-code, client-credentials and other grants, access and refresh tokens, and scopes. It is the base protocol for delegating access to a user's mail, calendar and files.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Nat Sakimura (ed.), John Bradley, Naveen Agarwal
title: Proof Key for Code Exchange by OAuth Public Clients (RFC 7636)
shows: Defines PKCE, which binds an authorization code to the client that requested it and so defeats code interception. Relevant to desktop and local agents that cannot keep a client secret.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Torsten Lodderstedt, John Bradley, Andrey Labunets, Daniel Fett
title: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security (RFC 9700, BCP 240)
shows: The current security best practice for OAuth 2.0, updating RFC 6749; it is the checklist to apply to an agent's token handling, including redirect matching, PKCE and token lifetime.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Torsten Lodderstedt (ed.), Mark McGloin, Phil Hunt
title: OAuth 2.0 Threat Model and Security Considerations (RFC 6819)
shows: A catalogue of threats against OAuth deployments and their countermeasures. It is a reference for threat-modelling an agent that stores long-lived refresh tokens.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: OWASP
title: A10:2021 Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), OWASP Top 10:2021
shows: Describes SSRF, where an application fetches an attacker-chosen URL, and the usual defences: allow-lists, blocking internal ranges and disabling redirects. An agent with a fetch or browse tool needs the same controls.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Stripe
title: Receive Stripe events in your webhook endpoint (signature verification)
shows: Documents signed webhooks: an HMAC over timestamp and raw body, constant-time comparison, a replay tolerance window, and duplicate-event handling. It is a worked example of authenticating inbound events that trigger agent actions.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: GitHub
title: Validating webhook deliveries
shows: Describes verifying an HMAC-SHA256 signature header against a shared secret with a constant-time comparison. A second independent reference for the same inbound-authentication pattern.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: OWASP GenAI Security Project
title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025
shows: Lists ten risks for LLM applications, including prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, improper output handling, excessive agency and data and model poisoning. A common industry vocabulary for reviewing an agent.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Model Context Protocol project
title: Security Best Practices (MCP specification)
shows: Lists MCP-specific attacks and mitigations: confused-deputy proxies, token passthrough, SSRF during OAuth discovery, local server compromise and scope minimisation. A primary source for securing a tool-protocol client.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Luca Beurer-Kellner, Marc Fischer
title: MCP Security Notification: Tool Poisoning Attacks
shows: Reports that instructions hidden in an MCP tool's description, which the model reads but the user typically does not, can steer an agent into actions the user did not approve. It shows that tool metadata is an untrusted input channel.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Brandon Radosevich, John Halloran
title: MCP Safety Audit: LLMs with the Model Context Protocol Allow Major Security Exploits
shows: Demonstrates that MCP-connected models can be induced to carry out several classes of exploit and introduces an auditing tool. An early academic assessment of MCP risk.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Zhiqiang Wang, Yichao Gao, Yanting Wang, Suyuan Liu, Haifeng Sun, Haoran Cheng, Guanquan Shi, Haohua Du, Xiangyang Li
title: MCPTox: A Benchmark for Tool Poisoning Attack on Real-World MCP Servers
shows: A benchmark measuring tool-poisoning success against real MCP servers across many models. It quantifies the risk described in the vendor advisories.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Zhaorun Chen, Zhen Xiang, Chaowei Xiao, Dawn Song, Bo Li
title: AgentPoison: Red-teaming LLM Agents via Poisoning Memory or Knowledge Bases
shows: Shows that a small number of poisoned entries in an agent's memory or knowledge base can be retrieved on trigger queries and redirect behaviour. It establishes memory stores as an attack surface.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Shen Dong, Shaochen Xu, Pengfei He, Yige Li, Jiliang Tang, Tianming Liu, Hui Liu, Zhen Xiang
title: Memory Injection Attacks on LLM Agents via Query-Only Interaction
shows: Shows that memory can be corrupted through query-only interaction, without direct access to the memory store. It argues for provenance and validation on memory writes.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Johann Rehberger (wunderwuzzi)
title: Bing Chat: Data Exfiltration Exploit Explained
shows: Documents data leaving a chat client because model-generated markdown images make the client request an external URL with data in the query string. It is the reference case for rendering and link-unfurl channels, and for blocking untrusted URLs in agent output.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Pavan Reddy, Aditya Sanjay Gujral
title: EchoLeak: The First Real-World Zero-Click Prompt Injection Exploit in a Production LLM System
shows: Case study of a zero-click prompt injection against a production LLM system. A realistic incident that exercises the lethal-trifecta conditions.
group: Protection, information flow and prompt injection

authors: Bradley Efron
title: Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife
shows: Introduces the bootstrap, a resampling method for estimating the sampling variability of a statistic without distributional assumptions. It is the basis for putting confidence intervals on eval scores computed from small task sets. (Verified via PDF whose JSTOR identifier matches this article plus a search record; the PDF text itself was not machine-readable.)

authors: A. Colin Cameron, Douglas L. Miller
title: A Practitioner's Guide to Cluster-Robust Inference
shows: Explains that default standard errors can badly overstate precision when observations are correlated within clusters, and gives cluster-robust remedies. Relevant when an agent eval has many trials per task or per user.

authors: Mary L. McHugh
title: Interrater reliability: the kappa statistic
shows: A tutorial on Cohen's kappa as a chance-corrected agreement measure, with interpretation thresholds and criticism of lenient benchmarks. Useful for measuring agreement between human labelers and between an LLM judge and humans.

authors: Yoav Benjamini, Yosef Hochberg
title: Controlling the False Discovery Rate: A Practical and Powerful Approach to Multiple Testing
venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B 57(1), 289-300
shows: Defines the false discovery rate and a procedure to control it when many hypotheses are tested. Applies when comparing many prompt or model variants on many metrics.

authors: Evan Miller
title: Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations
shows: Argues that eval results should be reported with standard errors and confidence intervals, and covers clustered errors, paired differences and power analysis for LLM evals. It is the most direct statistics primer for the course's eval work.

authors: Rotem Dror, Gili Baumer, Segev Shlomov, Roi Reichart
title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to Testing Statistical Significance in Natural Language Processing
shows: Surveys which significance tests suit which NLP evaluation settings and how to choose among them. Gives students a decision guide for comparing two systems.

authors: Thomas G. Dietterich
title: Approximate Statistical Tests for Comparing Supervised Classification Learning Algorithms
shows: Compares several tests for whether one learning algorithm beats another and measures their type I error. A classic on why naive comparisons of two systems can mislead.

authors: Ron Kohavi, Roger Longbotham, Dan Sommerfield, Randal M. Henne
title: Controlled Experiments on the Web: Survey and Practical Guide
shows: Surveys the design, statistics and pitfalls of randomized online controlled experiments from Amazon, Microsoft and others. It is the standard reference for testing a change to an agent on live traffic.

authors: Carlos E. Jimenez, John Yang, Alexander Wettig, Shunyu Yao, Kexin Pei, Ofir Press, Karthik Narasimhan
title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
shows: Introduces a benchmark of real GitHub issues in which a model must produce a patch that passes the repository's tests. It is the reference example of execution-based agent evaluation.

authors: Victor Barres, Honghua Dong, Soham Ray, Xujie Si, Karthik Narasimhan
title: tau2-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment
shows: Extends tau-bench to settings where both agent and user can act on a shared environment. Relevant for evaluating agents whose user also changes the world state.

authors: Ori Yoran, Samuel Joseph Amouyal, Chaitanya Malaviya, Ben Bogin, Ofir Press, Jonathan Berant
title: AssistantBench: Can Web Agents Solve Realistic and Time-Consuming Tasks?
shows: A benchmark of time-consuming information-seeking web tasks on the live web. It illustrates evaluation on a changing environment and low absolute scores for current agents.

authors: Xiao Liu, Hao Yu, Hanchen Zhang, Yifan Xu, Xuanyu Lei, Hanyu Lai, Yu Gu, Hangliang Ding, Kaiwen Men, Kejuan Yang, Shudan Zhang, Xiang Deng, Aohan Zeng, Zhengxiao Du, Chenhui Zhang, Sheng Shen, Tianjun Zhang, Yu Su, Huan Sun, Minlie Huang, Yuxiao Dong, Jie Tang
title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
shows: A multi-environment benchmark that tests LLMs as agents across several interactive settings. Shows how to span environment types in one suite.

authors: Frank F. Xu, Yufan Song, Boxuan Li, Yuxuan Tang, Kritanjali Jain, Mengxue Bao, Zora Z. Wang, Xuhui Zhou, Zhitong Guo, Murong Cao, Mingyang Yang, Hao Yang Lu, Amaad Martin, Zhe Su, Leander Maben, Raj Mehta, Wayne Chi, Lawrence Jang, Yiqing Xie, Shuyan Zhou, Graham Neubig
title: TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real World Tasks
shows: Simulates a software company with web, code and chat tools and simulated coworkers, and scores multi-step workplace tasks. It is an example of a benchmark with simulated people in a stateful environment.

authors: Sayash Kapoor, Benedikt Stroebl, Zachary S. Siegel, Nitya Nadgir, Arvind Narayanan
title: AI Agents That Matter
shows: Argues that agent evaluations should report cost alongside accuracy, separate model from downstream evaluation needs, guard against overfitting through holdouts, and fix reproducibility problems. It is the core critique for how to evaluate agents.

authors: Sayash Kapoor, Benedikt Stroebl, Peter Kirgis, Nitya Nadgir, Zachary S Siegel, Boyi Wei, et al.
title: Holistic Agent Leaderboard: The Missing Infrastructure for AI Agent Evaluation
shows: Describes shared infrastructure for running agent evaluations in a standardized way across benchmarks. Relevant to reproducible, cost-aware agent comparison.

authors: Yuxuan Zhu, Tengjun Jin, Yada Pruksachatkun, Andy Zhang, Shu Liu, Sasha Cui, Sayash Kapoor, Shayne Longpre, Kevin Meng, Rebecca Weiss, et al.
title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks
shows: Analyzes validity problems in existing agent benchmarks, including flaws in task setup and graders, and proposes a checklist for building them. A practical guide to what makes a benchmark trustworthy.

authors: You Wang, Michael Pradel, Zhongxin Liu
title: Are "Solved Issues" in SWE-bench Really Solved Correctly? An Empirical Study
shows: Empirically examines patches that pass SWE-bench's tests to see whether they are actually correct. An example of weak test-based graders inflating scores.

authors: Kun Zhou, Yutao Zhu, Zhipeng Chen, Wentong Chen, Wayne Xin Zhao, Xu Chen, Yankai Lin, Ji-Rong Wen, Jiawei Han
title: Don't Make Your LLM an Evaluation Benchmark Cheater
shows: Examines how benchmark data leaking into training inflates scores and distorts model comparison, and offers suggestions for fair evaluation. Introduces the contamination problem for the course.

authors: Benjamin Recht, Rebecca Roelofs, Ludwig Schmidt, Vaishaal Shankar
title: Do ImageNet Classifiers Generalize to ImageNet?
shows: Builds new test sets following the original ImageNet process and finds accuracy drops for existing classifiers, testing for adaptive overfitting to a reused test set. The standard citation for dev-set and test-set reuse risk.

authors: David Manheim, Scott Garrabrant
title: Categorizing Variants of Goodhart's Law
shows: Distinguishes several distinct ways optimizing a proxy measure can fail to improve the target. Gives vocabulary for how an optimized prompt or agent can overfit its metric.

authors: Leo Gao, John Schulman, Jacob Hilton
title: Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
shows: Measures how optimizing against a learned proxy reward eventually lowers the true reward, in how the gap scales with optimization. A quantitative case of Goodhart's law relevant to optimizing against LLM judges.

authors: Andrew M. Bean, Ryan Othniel Kearns, Angelika Romanou, et al.
title: Measuring what Matters: Construct Validity in Large Language Model Benchmarks
shows: A review of 445 LLM benchmarks against validity criteria that reports recurring weaknesses in what benchmarks measure and how they score it. Provides a checklist for judging whether a benchmark measures what it claims.

authors: Lianmin Zheng, Wei-Lin Chiang, Ying Sheng, Siyuan Zhuang, Zhanghao Wu, Yonghao Zhuang, Zi Lin, Zhuohan Li, Dacheng Li, Eric P. Xing, Hao Zhang, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Ion Stoica
title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
shows: Studies strong LLMs as judges, measures agreement with human preferences and documents position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases. The foundational paper for LLM-as-judge.

authors: Yang Liu, Dan Iter, Yichong Xu, Shuohang Wang, Ruochen Xu, Chenguang Zhu
title: G-Eval: NLG Evaluation using GPT-4 with Better Human Alignment
shows: Proposes prompting an LLM with criteria and generated evaluation steps to score text, and compares its correlation with human ratings. A reference design for rubric-based LLM grading.

authors: Shreya Shankar, J.D. Zamfirescu-Pereira, Bjorn Hartmann, Aditya G. Parameswaran, Ian Arawjo
title: Who Validates the Validators? Aligning LLM-Assisted Evaluation of LLM Outputs with Human Preferences
shows: A study of how people build and revise LLM-based evaluators, finding that evaluation criteria shift as people see outputs. It argues LLM judges need validation against human labels.

authors: Peiyi Wang, Lei Li, Liang Chen, Zefan Cai, Dawei Zhu, Binghuai Lin, Yunbo Cao, Qi Liu, Tianyu Liu, Zhifang Sui
title: Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators
shows: Shows that the order in which candidate answers are presented can change an LLM judge's verdict, and proposes calibration strategies. Evidence for randomizing or swapping order when judging.

authors: Arjun Panickssery, Samuel R. Bowman, Shi Feng
title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
shows: Finds that LLM evaluators can recognize their own outputs and that this recognition correlates with scoring them higher. Argues against using the same model as agent and judge.

authors: Stella Biderman, Hailey Schoelkopf, Lintang Sutawika, Leo Gao, Jonathan Tow, et al.
title: Lessons from the Trenches on Reproducible Evaluation of Language Models
shows: Reports practical sources of irreproducibility in LM evaluation (prompt formatting, implementation differences) from building the LM Evaluation Harness. Useful guidance on documenting and sharing eval setups.

authors: Melanie Sclar, Yejin Choi, Yulia Tsvetkov, Alane Suhr
title: Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting
shows: Measures how meaning-preserving changes to prompt format change measured model performance. Shows that single-prompt eval scores can have large hidden variance.

authors: Koen Claessen, John Hughes
title: QuickCheck: A lightweight tool for random testing of Haskell programs
shows: Introduces stating program properties as functions and testing them on randomly generated inputs. The origin of property-based testing, applicable to agent invariants such as idempotence or no-forbidden-action.

authors: Sergio Segura, Gordon Fraser, Ana B. Sanchez, Antonio Ruiz-Cortes
title: A Survey on Metamorphic Testing
shows: Surveys metamorphic testing, which checks relations between outputs under input transformations when no exact oracle exists. Relevant to testing agents whose correct output cannot be specified exactly.

authors: Tsong Yueh Chen, Fei-Ching Kuo, Huai Liu, Pak-Lok Poon, Dave Towey, T.H. Tse, Zhi Quan Zhou
title: Metamorphic Testing: A Review of Challenges and Opportunities
shows: A second review of metamorphic testing covering relation identification, test generation and open problems. Complements the 2016 survey.

authors: Marco Tulio Ribeiro, Tongshuang Wu, Carlos Guestrin, Sameer Singh
title: Beyond Accuracy: Behavioral Testing of NLP models with CheckList
shows: Proposes a task-agnostic methodology organizing tests by capability, with minimum-functionality, invariance and directional tests. A template for behavioral test suites for language-model systems.

authors: Ali Basiri, Niosha Behnam, Ruud de Rooij, Lorin Hochstein, Luke Kosewski, Justin Reynolds, Casey Rosenthal
title: Chaos Engineering
shows: Describes chaos engineering as experimenting on a production system to build confidence in its resilience to turbulent conditions. Motivates injecting tool failures and bad inputs into agents.

authors: Jepsen (Kyle Kingsbury)
title: Distributed Systems Safety Research (jepsen.io)
shows: The Jepsen project publishes analyses of distributed databases and maintains an open-source safety testing library. A model of adversarial, fault-injecting testing of systems against stated guarantees.

authors: Kyle Kingsbury, Peter Alvaro
title: Elle: Inferring Isolation Anomalies from Experimental Observations
shows: Describes a checker that infers isolation anomalies from recorded histories of a system under test. Illustrates separating generation of workloads from checking of recorded traces, a pattern usable on agent logs.

authors: Omar Khattab, Arnav Singhvi, Paridhi Maheshwari, Zhiyuan Zhang, Keshav Santhanam, Sri Vardhamanan, Saiful Haq, Ashutosh Sharma, Thomas T. Joshi, Hanna Moazam, Heather Miller, Matei Zaharia, Christopher Potts
title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
shows: Presents a programming model that expresses LM pipelines as modules and a compiler that optimizes their prompts and demonstrations against a metric. The basis for metric-driven prompt optimization.

authors: Lakshya A Agrawal, Shangyin Tan, Dilara Soylu, Noah Ziems, Rishi Khare, Krista Opsahl-Ong, Arnav Singhvi, Herumb Shandilya, Michael J Ryan, Meng Jiang, Christopher Potts, Koushik Sen, Alexandros G. Dimakis, Ion Stoica, Dan Klein, Matei Zaharia, Omar Khattab
title: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning
shows: Optimizes prompts by having an LLM reflect on execution traces in natural language and evolving candidates, and reports it can match or beat reinforcement learning with far fewer rollouts. Relevant to improving an agent from its own traces.

authors: Chengrun Yang, Xuezhi Wang, Yifeng Lu, Hanxiao Liu, Quoc V. Le, Denny Zhou, Xinyun Chen
title: Large Language Models as Optimizers
shows: Introduces OPRO, which uses an LLM to propose new solutions given a history of earlier solutions and their scores, applied to prompt optimization. An early example of metric-driven prompt search.

authors: Mert Yuksekgonul, Federico Bianchi, Joseph Boen, Sheng Liu, Zhi Huang, Carlos Guestrin, James Zou
title: TextGrad: Automatic "Differentiation" via Text
shows: Backpropagates natural-language feedback from an LLM through a computation graph of LLM calls to improve variables such as prompts. Another approach to optimizing compound systems.

authors: Krista Opsahl-Ong, Michael J Ryan, Josh Purtell, David Broman, Christopher Potts, Matei Zaharia, Omar Khattab
title: Optimizing Instructions and Demonstrations for Multi-Stage Language Model Programs
shows: Presents MIPRO, which jointly optimizes instructions and few-shot demonstrations across the modules of a multi-stage LM program. Used to discuss search budget and dev-set overfitting.

authors: Alex Tamkin, Miles McCain, Kunal Handa, Esin Durmus, Liane Lovitt, Ankur Rathi, Saffron Huang, Alfred Mountfield, Jerry Hong, Stuart Ritchie, Michael Stern, Brian Clarke, Landon Goldberg, Theodore R. Sumers, Jared Mueller, William McEachen, Wes Mitchell, Shan Carter, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Deep Ganguli
title: Clio: Privacy-Preserving Insights into Real-World AI Use
shows: Describes an automated pipeline that clusters and summarizes real conversations with privacy protections so usage patterns can be studied without reading individual chats. A model for analyzing an agent's own production traces while limiting exposure of personal data.

authors: Mikaela Grace, Jeremy Hadfield, Rodrigo Olivares, Jiri De Jonghe
title: Demystifying evals for AI agents
shows: A model maker's guide that defines evals, discusses code-based, model-based and human graders for multi-turn agents, and covers pass@k and pass^k for non-deterministic results. Official practical guidance for building agent evals.

authors: Anthropic
title: Define success criteria and build evaluations
shows: Official documentation on defining measurable success criteria and building automated evaluations, including exact-match, similarity and LLM-based grading methods. A baseline for designing an eval set for an application.

authors: OpenAI
title: Evaluation best practices
shows: A model maker's guide that explains why variable generative output needs evals and describes a five-step workflow comparing metric-based, human and LLM-judge evaluators. Notes from a search result (not verified on the opened page) say the OpenAI Evals platform is being deprecated, so check the page before assigning.

authors: Anthropic
title: Prompt caching
shows: Documents caching of prompt prefixes via cache_control with 5-minute and 1-hour lifetimes. States cache writes cost 1.25x (5-minute) or 2x (1-hour) of base input price and reads cost 0.1x or less, which drives agent cost and latency design.

authors: George Candea, Armando Fox
title: Crash-Only Software
shows: Proposes building components so that the only way to stop them is to crash them and the only way to start them is to recover. A personal agent that must survive restarts can adopt this so that every shutdown path is the recovery path.

authors: Joe Armstrong
title: Making reliable distributed systems in the presence of software errors
venue: PhD dissertation, Royal Institute of Technology (KTH), Stockholm
shows: Describes structuring a system as isolated communicating processes with supervisors that restart failed workers, on the premise that software contains errors. Gives the vocabulary behind supervision trees and let-it-crash for long-running agents.

authors: Jim Gray
title: Why Do Computers Stop and What Can Be Done About It?
shows: Analyses failure reports from a commercial fault-tolerant system and finds administration and software dominate outages, with many software faults transient. Motivates restart-and-retry, process pairs and transactions as design tools.

authors: Jay Kreps
title: The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction
shows: Presents the append-only, ordered log as the basis for data integration and replicated state. Supports designing an agent's journal as the source of truth from which other state is derived.

authors: Martin Fowler
title: Event Sourcing
shows: Explains recording every state change as an ordered event and rebuilding or correcting state by replaying events. Gives a pattern for an append-only journal that can be replayed after a restart.

authors: Martin Kleppmann
title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
shows: Textbook treatment of reliability, replication, transactions, logs, stream processing and exactly-once effects. Serves as the general reference for the storage and delivery questions an agent's runtime raises.

authors: Leslie Lamport
title: Time, clocks, and the ordering of events in a distributed system
shows: Defines the happened-before relation and logical clocks as a way to order events without a shared physical clock. Relevant when an agent's journal merges events from several chat, email and scheduler sources.

authors: Jim Waldo, Geoff Wyant, Ann Wollrath, Sam Kendall
title: A note on distributed computing
venue: Mobile Object Systems: Towards the Programmable Internet, Lecture Notes in Computer Science 1222 (first issued as Sun Microsystems Laboratories TR-94-29, 1994)
shows: Argues that remote calls differ fundamentally from local ones in latency, partial failure and concurrency, so interfaces must not hide the network. Basis for treating every call an agent makes to an external account as fallible.

authors: Marc Brooker
title: Exponential Backoff And Jitter
shows: Compares retry strategies with and without randomised delay under contention and recommends adding jitter to exponential backoff. Directly applicable to how an agent retries failing account APIs without hammering them.

authors: Pat Helland
title: Idempotence Is Not a Medical Condition
venue: ACM Queue / Communications of the ACM
shows: Explains why messages are delivered at least once in practice and how applications must tolerate duplicates through idempotent processing. Core reasoning for safe retries of side-effecting agent actions.

authors: Pat Helland
title: Life Beyond Distributed Transactions
shows: Argues that scalable applications confine transactions to single entities and coordinate across them with messages and tolerance for duplicates. Offers a model for agents that act across independent services with no shared transaction.

authors: Pat Helland
title: Immutability changes everything
shows: Argues that append-only, immutable data simplifies replication and reasoning about history, with derived views built on top. Supports an append-only journal design.

authors: Jeffrey Dean, Luiz Andre Barroso
title: The tail at scale
shows: Shows how rare slow responses dominate end-to-end latency in large systems and describes hedged and tied requests. Useful for reasoning about timeouts and duplicate requests when an agent depends on slow external services.

authors: Stripe
title: Idempotent requests
shows: Documents the idempotency-key pattern: a client-chosen key lets a request be retried after a connection error without repeating its effect. A concrete, widely used design for making an agent's outgoing actions safe to retry.

authors: Google SRE book authors (chapter-level authorship not verified)
title: Embracing Risk
venue: Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems, ch. 3, O'Reilly
shows: Introduces error budgets: accepting a stated amount of unreliability so that change can proceed. Gives a method for deciding how much failure an unattended agent may be allowed before it is stopped.

authors: Google SRE book authors (chapter-level authorship not verified)
title: Service Level Objectives
shows: Defines indicators, objectives and agreements and how to choose them. Lets an agent project state measurable targets for things like missed scheduled runs.

authors: Google SRE book authors (chapter-level authorship not verified)
title: Monitoring Distributed Systems
shows: Describes the four golden signals and argues that alerts should be actionable and symptom-based. Applies to deciding what an unattended agent should report and what it should only log.

authors: Google SRE book authors (chapter-level authorship not verified)
title: Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure
shows: Describes blameless written postmortems with causes and follow-up actions. Suggests a template for reviewing agent incidents recorded in its own journal.

authors: D. L. Parnas
title: On the criteria to be used in decomposing systems into modules
shows: Shows that modules should be cut around design decisions likely to change rather than around processing steps. Guides separating an agent's channel, account and journal components so each can be replaced.

authors: Frederick P. Brooks Jr.
title: No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering
shows: Distinguishes essential from accidental complexity and argues no single technique will give an order-of-magnitude gain. A counterweight to expecting a model alone to remove the engineering work around an agent.

authors: Butler W. Lampson
title: Hints for computer system design
shows: Collects practical design advice on simplicity, interfaces, logs, atomic actions and making operations idempotent. A compact general reference for the agent runtime.

authors: Hector Garcia-Molina, Kenneth Salem
title: Sagas
shows: Proposes splitting a long-lived transaction into steps, each with a compensating action. Relevant to multi-step agent tasks across accounts that cannot be rolled back atomically.

authors: David Thomas, Andrew Hunt
title: The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th Anniversary Edition
venue: Pragmatic Bookshelf (book; tracer bullets first appeared in the 1999 edition)
shows: Source of the 'tracer bullets' technique: build a thin end-to-end path first and refine it. Applies to building the chat-to-account-to-journal loop before any breadth.

authors: D. Sculley, Gary Holt, Daniel Golovin, Eugene Davydov, Todd Phillips, Dietmar Ebner, Vinay Chaudhary, Michael Young, Jean-Francois Crespo, Dan Dennison
title: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 28 (NeurIPS 2015)
shows: Catalogues system-level maintenance costs in ML systems such as entanglement, hidden feedback loops and glue code. Warns about the surrounding code a model-driven agent accumulates.

authors: Richard S. Sutton
title: The Bitter Lesson
shows: Argues that general methods that use more computation have beaten hand-built domain knowledge over the long run. Used to discuss which parts of an agent to hand-code and which to leave to the model.

authors: R. H. Coase
title: The Nature of the Firm
shows: Explains the boundary of the firm by the cost of using the market versus organising internally. The root of the make-or-buy question when choosing whether to build or rent an agent component.

authors: Oliver E. Williamson
title: Transaction-Cost Economics: The Governance of Contractual Relations
venue: The Journal of Law and Economics
shows: Develops transaction-cost economics, showing how asset specificity and uncertainty determine whether to buy or integrate. Gives vocabulary for vendor lock-in and dependency decisions.

authors: Saleema Amershi, Dan Weld, Mihaela Vorvoreanu, Adam Fourney, Besmira Nushi, Penny Collisson, Jina Suh, Shamsi Iqbal, Paul N. Bennett, Kori Inkpen, Jaime Teevan, and others
title: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction
shows: Presents 18 guidelines for AI-infused systems, derived from prior work and tested with practitioners. A checklist for reviewing the agent's conversational behaviour.

authors: Raja Parasuraman, Thomas B. Sheridan, Christopher D. Wickens
title: A model for types and levels of human interaction with automation
venue: IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics - Part A
shows: Proposes that automation varies by level across four stages: information acquisition, analysis, decision and action. Gives a vocabulary for setting how autonomous the agent is for each kind of task.

authors: John D. Lee, Katrina A. See
title: Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance
shows: Reviews trust in automation and argues that design should aim at calibrated reliance rather than maximum trust. Informs what an agent should show about its own reliability.

authors: Gary Klein, David D. Woods, Jeffrey M. Bradshaw, Robert R. Hoffman, Paul J. Feltovich
title: Ten Challenges for Making Automation a "Team Player" in Joint Human-Agent Activity
shows: Lists requirements for automation to cooperate with people, such as keeping common ground and making its actions and intentions observable. Relevant to what an agent reports in chat.

authors: Edwin L. Hutchins, James D. Hollan, Donald A. Norman
title: Direct Manipulation Interfaces
shows: Analyses interfaces in terms of the gulfs of execution and evaluation between user goals and system state. Used to frame feedback an agent owes after acting on a person's behalf.

authors: Mark Weiser, John Seely Brown
title: The Coming Age of Calm Technology
venue: Xerox PARC essay (reprinted in Beyond Calculation, Springer, 1997)
shows: Argues that technology should move between the centre and periphery of attention rather than demand it. Frames the design of notifications from a long-running agent.

authors: Herbert H. Clark, Susan E. Brennan
title: Grounding in communication
venue: Perspectives on Socially Shared Cognition, American Psychological Association
shows: Describes how conversation partners establish mutual understanding and repair misunderstandings at a cost depending on the medium. Basis for clarification and confirmation behaviour in an agent chat.

authors: Gloria Mark, Daniela Gudith, Ulrich Klocke
title: The cost of interrupted work
shows: Reports an experiment in which interrupted workers finished faster but with more stress and effort. Evidence that unprompted agent messages have a cost.

authors: Mary Czerwinski, Eric Horvitz, Susan Wilhite
title: A diary study of task switching and interruptions
shows: Diary study of how knowledge workers experience switching and interruption, including difficulty resuming tasks. Informs when an agent should defer a message.

authors: Eric Horvitz, Andy Jacobs, David Hovel
title: Attention-Sensitive Alerting
shows: Casts alert delivery as a decision weighing the value of information against the cost of interruption given the user's attention. Gives a formal basis for an agent's notification policy.

authors: Vannevar Bush
title: As We May Think
shows: Proposes the memex, a personal device for storing and linking a person's records. Historical statement of the personal-memory aim an agent's journal serves.

authors: J. C. R. Licklider
title: Man-Computer Symbiosis
venue: IRE Transactions on Human Factors in Electronics
shows: Envisions a division of labour in which computers handle routine work and preparation so people can focus on formulating and judging. Early statement of the delegation model behind personal agents.

authors: Pattie Maes
title: Agents that reduce work and information overload
shows: Describes personal software agents that learn a user's habits to handle email, meetings and filtering, and discusses trust and control. Early model for an agent that learns what to do for one person.

authors: Karen Myers, Pauline Berry, Jim Blythe, Ken Conley, Melinda Gervasio, Deborah McGuinness, David Morley, Avi Pfeffer, Martha Pollack, Milind Tambe
title: An Intelligent Personal Assistant for Task and Time Management
shows: Describes a deployed assistant from the CALO project that manages time commitments and tasks for a knowledge worker. Primary example of a personal assistant built from a task-execution architecture.

authors: Steve Whittaker, Candace Sidner
title: Email overload
shows: Studies how people use mailboxes as to-do lists and archives and describes why they become overloaded. Informs what an agent can triage and what it must leave in view.

authors: Victoria Bellotti, Nicolas Ducheneaut, Mark Howard, Ian Smith
title: Taking email to task
shows: Presents and evaluates an email tool organised around tasks rather than messages. Evidence for task-centred handling of mail by an assistant.

authors: Justin Cranshaw, Emad Elwany, Todd Newman, Rafal Kocielnik, Bowen Yu, Sandeep Soni, Jaime Teevan, Andres Monroy-Hernandez
title: Calendar.help: Designing a Workflow-Based Scheduling Agent with Humans in the Loop
shows: Describes a meeting-scheduling agent that splits email scheduling into micro-tasks done by software and people. Case study on the limits of fully automatic scheduling.

authors: Ivan P. Fellegi, Alan B. Sunter
title: A Theory for Record Linkage
venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association
shows: Gives the probabilistic framework for deciding whether two records refer to the same entity using match and non-match weights. Foundation for linking contacts across a person's accounts.

authors: Ahmed K. Elmagarmid, Panagiotis G. Ipeirotis, Vassilios S. Verykios
title: Duplicate Record Detection: A Survey
venue: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering
shows: Surveys techniques for field matching and duplicate detection. Overview reading for CRM-style contact deduplication.

authors: George Papadakis, Dimitrios Skoutas, Emmanouil Thanos, Themis Palpanas
title: Blocking and Filtering Techniques for Entity Resolution
shows: Surveys methods that cut the number of record pairs compared in entity resolution. Relevant when contact and company data grows beyond pairwise comparison.

authors: Yiheng Xu, Minghao Li, Lei Cui, Shaohan Huang, Furu Wei, Ming Zhou
title: LayoutLM: Pre-training of Text and Layout for Document Image Understanding
shows: Introduces joint pre-training on text and page layout for tasks such as form and receipt understanding. Representative of model-based extraction from scanned documents.
